Reference: Langer and Lemoine (2022)

Model Setting

The paper asks how a regulator should shape the time path of a subsidy for a durable technology when she wants to reach a given level of adoption by a given date and dislikes spending public funds. Potential adopters have heterogeneous, privately known values, each adopts at most once and then leaves the market, the technology becomes cheaper over time, and the regulator commits at date 0 to an announced schedule. Subsidies of this kind (solar panels, electric vehicles, efficient appliances, electronic medical records) are in practice flat or declining. The theory shows that the regulator faces a tension. Intertemporal price discrimination calls for a subsidy that rises over time: a low early subsidy collects the high-value households cheaply and a higher later subsidy brings in the low-value ones, so that inframarginal adopters are not overpaid. Against this, households who anticipate the schedule can wait for the higher subsidy, which limits price discrimination (an information rent), and technological progress, a preference for smooth spending, and the flow benefit of earlier adoption all push towards a flatter or declining path. The paper does not state numbered propositions; its theoretical result is a single differential equation for the efficient subsidy whose numerator is decomposed, term by term, into named channels. The regulator's subsidy is called "efficient" rather than "optimal" because the adoption target itself is not derived from welfare.

The quantitative part estimates a dynamic discrete choice model of residential solar adoption under the California Solar Initiative (CSI), in which the subsidy fell in steps from 2.50 dollars per watt to zero while pre-subsidy system costs fell from about 9 to about 4 dollars per watt, and then computes the efficient schedule for a calibrated regulator. The efficient subsidy increases over time in every baseline case, and no reasonable variation reproduces the sharply declining CSI path unless the regulator values solar electricity about 50 times more than standard estimates. Household foresight is expensive for the regulator: with improving technology, the present value of spending is 120 million dollars when households are forward looking and 24 million dollars when they are myopic, a fivefold difference.

The Regulator

The regulator knows the distribution of values but not any household's value, and all adopters in a period receive the same subsidy, so she cannot discriminate within a period. Her distaste for spending is G(st[Qt+1−Qt])>0G(s_t[Q_{t+1}-Q_t])>0G(st​[Qt+1​−Qt​])>0, with G(⋅)G(\cdot)G(⋅) strictly increasing and strictly convex. Convexity of the cost of public funds stands for political constraints, a deadweight loss of taxation that rises nonlinearly with revenue, administrative costs, or per-period budgets (CSI funds were collected from electricity bills on a rolling basis). She also receives a flow benefit B(Qt)>0B(Q_t)>0B(Qt​)>0 from cumulative adoption, with B(⋅)B(\cdot)B(⋅) weakly increasing and weakly concave. At date 0 she chooses {st}t=0T\{s_t\}_{t=0}^T{st​}t=0T​ to maximize:

∑t=0T(1+r)−t E0[B(Qt)−G(st[Qt+1−Qt])](3)\sum_{t=0}^{T}(1+r)^{-t}\,\mathbb{E}_0\left[B(Q_t)-G\left(s_t[Q_{t+1}-Q_t]\right)\right] \tag{3}t=0∑T​(1+r)−tE0​[B(Qt​)−G(st​[Qt+1​−Qt​])](3)

for discount rate r>0r>0r>0 and initial adoption Q0≥0Q_0\geq0Q0​≥0, subject to expected terminal adoption E0[QT+1]\mathbb{E}_0[Q_{T+1}]E0​[QT+1​] being at least the target Q^>Q0\hat{Q}>Q_0Q^​>Q0​. Households expect the subsidy to drop to zero after TTT. As B′(⋅)B'(\cdot)B′(⋅) and G′′(⋅)G''(\cdot)G′′(⋅) jointly go to zero the problem becomes one of minimizing the present cost of spending (the cost-effective subsidy), which is the durable-goods monopoly problem of Stokey (1979) and Landsberger and Meilijson (1985) in which intertemporal discrimination may not pay. Either a benefit from the stock of adoption or a convex cost of funds is enough to spread adoption over time.

Continuous-Time Specialization

The analysis specializes the setting in two ways that remove expectations: technological progress is deterministic, so cost is C(t,Q(t))C(t,Q(t))C(t,Q(t)), and preferences are fixed, so values are viv_ivi​. Here J(vi,C(T,Q^))J(v_i,C(T,\hat{Q}))J(vi​,C(T,Q^​)) is the present value to household iii of the option to adopt after TTT, when the subsidy has disappeared for good: a household that has not yet adopted does so at TTT if and only if vi−C(T,Q^)+s(T)≥J(vi,C(T,Q^))v_i-C(T,\hat{Q})+s(T)\geq J(v_i,C(T,\hat{Q}))vi​−C(T,Q^​)+s(T)≥J(vi​,C(T,Q^​)). The initial subsidy s0s_0s0​ is free, so the subsidy is a state variable with a free initial value, and its costate is zero at date 0.

The plan is time inconsistent. The date-0 regulator promises a moderate subsidy at ttt partly to keep households at earlier dates w<tw<tw<t from waiting; once ttt arrives those decisions are sunk and she would like to offer more. The paper does not model the game without commitment (the Coase conjecture literature) and follows the dynamic public finance tradition of assuming commitment, arguing that legislated schedules defined over time or cumulative adoption, as in California, were in fact honored. Commitment is what allows any price discrimination against forward-looking households, but its value is not quantified. Because the model is deterministic, it does not matter whether the schedule is written as a function of ttt or of Q(t)Q(t)Q(t).

The Efficient Subsidy Path

The paper's appendix A (online) derives the necessary conditions. At times with strictly positive adoption, y(t)<0y(t)<0y(t)<0, the efficient subsidy evolves as:

s˙(t)=[rs(t)G′f(Y(t))−B′f(Y(t))+G′Q˙(t)−μ˙(t)+rμ(t)−[s(t)]2G′′f(Y(t))Q¨(t)+G′Q˙(t)C2(t,Q(t))f(Y(t))]×[G′f(Y(t))+s(t)f(Y(t))G′′Q˙(t)]−1(13)\begin{aligned} \dot{s}(t)=\Big[&rs(t)G'f(Y(t))-B'f(Y(t))+G'\dot{Q}(t)-\dot{\mu}(t)+r\mu(t)\\ &-[s(t)]^2G''f(Y(t))\ddot{Q}(t)+G'\dot{Q}(t)C_2(t,Q(t))f(Y(t))\Big]\\ &\times\Big[G'f(Y(t))+s(t)f(Y(t))G''\dot{Q}(t)\Big]^{-1} \end{aligned} \tag{13}s˙(t)=[​rs(t)G′f(Y(t))−B′f(Y(t))+G′Q˙​(t)−μ˙​(t)+rμ(t)−[s(t)]2G′′f(Y(t))Q¨​(t)+G′Q˙​(t)C2​(t,Q(t))f(Y(t))]×[G′f(Y(t))+s(t)f(Y(t))G′′Q˙​(t)]−1​(13)

where G′G'G′, G′′G''G′′ and B′B'B′ are evaluated at current spending and adoption, and the costate μ(t)≥0\mu(t)\geq0μ(t)≥0 on the incentive constraint measures the cost of keeping promises made to those who adopted in the past, with μ(0)=0\mu(0)=0μ(0)=0 as the transversality condition for the free s0s_0s0​. The denominator is positive, so the sign of s˙(t)\dot{s}(t)s˙(t) is the sign of the numerator, and each term is a channel.

  • Hotelling channel, rs(t)G′f(Y(t))>0rs(t)G'f(Y(t))>0rs(t)G′f(Y(t))>0: an impatient regulator wants to delay spending, so for her to be indifferent to shifting a marginal adopter across instants the cost of spending must grow at rate rrr. Favors an increasing subsidy.

Favors an increasing subsidy, more strongly the larger the mass of inframarginal adopters and the marginal cost of funds.

  • Promise-keeping terms, −μ˙(t)≤0-\dot{\mu}(t)\leq0−μ˙​(t)≤0 and rμ(t)≥0r\mu(t)\geq0rμ(t)≥0: present only when households are forward looking. These are the signs stated in the paper; the first need not hold when δ>r\delta>rδ>r, and only the three terms together, which equal δμ(t)\delta\mu(t)δμ(t), are signed.

  • Smooth spending channel, −[s(t)]2G′′f(Y(t))Q¨(t)-[s(t)]^2G''f(Y(t))\ddot{Q}(t)−[s(t)]2G′′f(Y(t))Q¨​(t): with a convex cost of funds, rising instantaneous adoption calls for a falling subsidy.

  • Endogenous cost channel, G′Q˙(t)C2(t,Q(t))f(Y(t))≤0G'\dot{Q}(t)C_2(t,Q(t))f(Y(t))\leq0G′Q˙​(t)C2​(t,Q(t))f(Y(t))≤0: early adoption lowers the net cost faced by later adopters. Favors a decreasing subsidy.

The logic of the first two channels is a perturbation argument. Suppose the marginal cost of funds is one and C2=0C_2=0C2​=0, and let the regulator shift the marginal type by ϵ\epsilonϵ, which moves a mass ϵf(Y(t))\epsilon f(Y(t))ϵf(Y(t)) of adoption from ttt to t+Δtt+\Delta tt+Δt. She saves ϵs(t)f(Y(t))\epsilon s(t)f(Y(t))ϵs(t)f(Y(t)) today, earns interest at rate rrr, loses the benefit flow B′B'B′ on the delayed adoption, and pays ϵs(t+Δt)f(Y(t))\epsilon s(t+\Delta t)f(Y(t))ϵs(t+Δt)f(Y(t)) later. Indifference as Δt→0\Delta t\to0Δt→0 gives:

Foresight and Constrained Price Discrimination

The costate equation is:

−μ˙(t)+rμ(t)=−G′Q˙(t)+δμ(t)(15)-\dot{\mu}(t)+r\mu(t)=-G'\dot{Q}(t)+\delta\mu(t) \tag{15}−μ˙​(t)+rμ(t)=−G′Q˙​(t)+δμ(t)(15)

so the promise-keeping terms exactly offset the price discrimination channel and leave only δμ(t)≥0\delta\mu(t)\geq0δμ(t)≥0, the constrained price discrimination channel. Substituting into the efficient path:

s˙(t)=rs(t)G′f(Y(t))−B′f(Y(t))+δμ(t)−[s(t)]2G′′f(Y(t))Q¨(t)+G′Q˙(t)C2(t,Q(t))f(Y(t))G′f(Y(t))+s(t)f(Y(t))G′′Q˙(t)(16)\dot{s}(t)=\frac{rs(t)G'f(Y(t))-B'f(Y(t))+\delta\mu(t)-[s(t)]^2G''f(Y(t))\ddot{Q}(t)+G'\dot{Q}(t)C_2(t,Q(t))f(Y(t))}{G'f(Y(t))+s(t)f(Y(t))G''\dot{Q}(t)} \tag{16}s˙(t)=G′f(Y(t))+s(t)f(Y(t))G′′Q˙​(t)rs(t)G′f(Y(t))−B′f(Y(t))+δμ(t)−[s(t)]2G′′f(Y(t))Q¨​(t)+G′Q˙​(t)C2​(t,Q(t))f(Y(t))​(16)

Solving the costate equation forward from μ(0)=0\mu(0)=0μ(0)=0:

μ(t)=∫0te−(δ−r)(t−i)G′Q˙(i) di(17)\mu(t)=\int_0^te^{-(\delta-r)(t-i)}G'\dot{Q}(i)\,di \tag{17}μ(t)=∫0t​e−(δ−r)(t−i)G′Q˙​(i)di(17)

The interpretation is that, with forward-looking households, the inframarginal adopters relevant for the subsidy at ttt include everyone who adopted earlier: raising s(t)s(t)s(t) by a dollar tempts earlier adopters to wait, so earlier subsidies must rise too. They need not rise by a full dollar, because households are impatient, and the weight on an adopter of date iii decays at rate δ−r\delta-rδ−r. The larger is δ\deltaδ, the more the regulator can price discriminate. Two implications follow. First, since μ(0)=0\mu(0)=0μ(0)=0, the channel vanishes at the initial date: anticipation removes price discrimination in the first instants and tilts the early subsidy path downward. In mechanism-design terms, high-value households can mimic low-value ones by waiting, incentive compatibility limits discrimination, and the vanishing of the channel at date 0 is the familiar "no distortion at the top"; the channel grows over time because lower types can extract less information rent. Second, as households become myopic, μ(t)→0\mu(t)\to0μ(t)→0 and μ˙(t)→0\dot{\mu}(t)\to0μ˙​(t)→0, and the integral expression implies:

lim⁡δ→∞δμ(t)=G′Q˙(t)(18)\lim_{\delta\to\infty}\delta\mu(t)=G'\dot{Q}(t) \tag{18}δ→∞lim​δμ(t)=G′Q˙​(t)(18)

for t>0t>0t>0, so the full price discrimination channel is restored. Foresight therefore flattens an increasing subsidy and, because the subsidy must also compensate households for giving up the option to adopt later, raises its level.

Smooth Spending, Technical Change and Endogenous Cost

The smooth spending channel depends on how instantaneous adoption changes over time:

Q¨(t)=−f(Y(t))y˙(t)−f′(Y(t))[y(t)]2(19)\ddot{Q}(t)=-f(Y(t))\dot{y}(t)-f'(Y(t))[y(t)]^2 \tag{19}Q¨​(t)=−f(Y(t))y˙​(t)−f′(Y(t))[y(t)]2(19)

If y˙(t)<0\dot{y}(t)<0y˙​(t)<0, the measure of types for which adoption becomes optimal is growing, which is plausible when progress, peer effects or network effects raise the value of adopting over time. If f′(Y(t))<0f'(Y(t))<0f′(Y(t))<0, the marginal type is moving from the upper tail into a thicker part of the distribution, as one expects for a new technology. In both cases spending tends to rise over time, and a regulator with G′′>0G''>0G′′>0 leans against this with a declining subsidy. The channel vanishes when the marginal cost of funds is constant.

Anticipated cost declines act through three routes. They raise adoption at a given subsidy and hence the number of inframarginal adopters, which strengthens price discrimination and favors an increasing subsidy. They strengthen the smooth spending channel through y(t)y(t)y(t) and y˙(t)\dot{y}(t)y˙​(t), which favors a decreasing subsidy. And they lower the level of the subsidy needed later, which weakens the Hotelling channel and again favors a decreasing subsidy. The net effect is an empirical matter. Endogenous cost, C2<0C_2<0C2​<0, adds an unambiguous force for a high early subsidy, whether it reflects induced technical change or peer effects.

Three extensions are reported from the online appendix E. With a fixed budget instead of a fixed target the necessary conditions are unchanged, apart from the transversality condition and the marginal cost of funds being scaled up by the shadow cost of the budget. With a linear cost of funds, G′′=0G''=0G′′=0, the objective is linear in y(t)y(t)y(t) and a bang-bang solution with all adoption at TTT is possible, but the efficient path still obeys the same equation when B′B'B′ is large enough relative to the marginal cost of funds. For a welfare-maximizing regulator who counts household surplus, the dynamics are qualitatively the same when the subsidy is financed by distortionary taxes, and the price discrimination channel disappears under a costless lump-sum tax; the main difference is the choice of Q^\hat{Q}Q^​.

Empirical Setting and Data

The CSI subsidized residential solar from 2007 to 2014, spending 2.2 billion dollars for 1,940 megawatts across Pacific Gas and Electric (PG&E), Southern California Edison (SCE) and San Diego Gas and Electric (SDG&E). The subsidy started at 2.50 dollars per watt and stepped down to zero, with steps triggered by cumulative adoption thresholds in each utility; a 30 percent federal tax credit was also available. The data combine CSI applications (date, zip code, utility, subsidy, system size and cost), utility rate schedules (the average marginal price for usage above 200 percent of baseline, at which net metering values solar output), American Community Survey block-group demographics of owner-occupied households, precinct vote shares, and zip-code solar radiation. System cost is the monthly average cost per watt in each utility times the median system size of 5.4 kilowatts. There are 4,104,377 owner-occupied households and 49,765 installations. The estimation window starts in January 2009, when the cap on the federal credit was removed, and ends before the subsidy expires in PG&E, for 41 months (the count in the estimates table; the dates stated in the text, January 2009 to March 2012, span 39 months).

Dynamic Discrete Choice Model

The empirical model parameterizes the discrete-time stopping problem above, without the simplifications of the theory. Each month a household that has not adopted decides whether to install a system of average size. The shocks ε⃗it\vec{\varepsilon}_{it}εit​ are i.i.d. type I extreme value, and the value of solar, interpreted as the expected present value of the stream of benefits plus the up-front non-monetary net benefit of installing, is:

hit=Xit′γ(20)h_{it}=X_{it}'\gamma \tag{20}hit​=Xit′​γ(20)

where XitX_{it}Xit​ contains a constant, solar radiation, the electricity price, log home value, years of schooling, utility fixed effects and a quadratic time trend that stands for improving system quality (and possibly peer effects). Money enters through a household-specific marginal utility αi<0\alpha_i<0αi​<0 applied to the net-of-subsidy cost:

C~it≜(1−ϕ)Cit−sit(21)\tilde{C}_{it}\triangleq(1-\phi)C_{it}-s_{it} \tag{21}C~it​≜(1−ϕ)Cit​−sit​(21)

where ϕ\phiϕ is the fraction of cost covered by the federal subsidy and costs and subsidies vary by utility. This assumes full pass-through of the CSI subsidy. The state variables are the system cost, the month (which indexes the known subsidy and electricity price paths and the time trend) and the fixed household characteristics. Cost follows an exogenous first-order Markov process that households know:

Ci(t+1)=κ0+κ1Cit+ωit(22)C_{i(t+1)}=\kappa_0+\kappa_1C_{it}+\omega_{it} \tag{22}Ci(t+1)​=κ0​+κ1​Cit​+ωit​(22)

with ωit\omega_{it}ωit​ normally distributed. Households know the full time path of subsidies and of preference shifters such as electricity prices from the start of the window, and have rational expectations over cost; in particular they are assumed to know the dates at which the adoption-triggered subsidy steps occur. Finally, many households cannot install solar at all (multi-family dwellings, unsuitable roofs), so each household is able to consider solar with probability ζi\zeta_iζi​, a permanent random shock. Conditional on considering solar, the logit shocks give the adoption probability:

Pit=exp⁡(Xit′γ+αiC~it)exp⁡(Xit′γ+αiC~it)+exp⁡(β E[V(Ωt+1,ε⃗i(t+1))∣Ωt])(23)P_{it}=\frac{\exp\left(X_{it}'\gamma+\alpha_i\tilde{C}_{it}\right)}{\exp\left(X_{it}'\gamma+\alpha_i\tilde{C}_{it}\right)+\exp\left(\beta\,\mathbb{E}\left[V(\Omega_{t+1},\vec{\varepsilon}_{i(t+1)})\mid\Omega_t\right]\right)} \tag{23}Pit​=exp(Xit′​γ+αi​C~it​)+exp(βE[V(Ωt+1​,εi(t+1)​)∣Ωt​])exp(Xit′​γ+αi​C~it​)​(23)

Estimation and Identification

The model is estimated by maximum likelihood with a nested fixed point. The likelihood of period ttt over the NtN_tNt​ households that have not yet installed is:

Lt=∏i=1Nt{[ζiPit]1{i adopts in t}[(1−ζi)+ζi(1−Pit)]1{i does not adopt in t}}(24)L_t=\prod_{i=1}^{N_t}\Big\{\left[\zeta_iP_{it}\right]^{1\{i\text{ adopts in }t\}}\left[(1-\zeta_i)+\zeta_i(1-P_{it})\right]^{1\{i\text{ does not adopt in }t\}}\Big\} \tag{24}Lt​=i=1∏Nt​​{[ζi​Pit​]1{i adopts in t}[(1−ζi​)+ζi​(1−Pit​)]1{i does not adopt in t}}(24)

so a household adopts with the probability of considering solar times the conditional adoption probability, and does not adopt either because it cannot consider solar or because it considers and declines. The paper prints the continuation term in the likelihood as exp⁡(β E[V(Ωt+1∣Ωt)])\exp(\beta\,\mathbb{E}[V(\Omega_{t+1}\mid\Omega_t)])exp(βE[V(Ωt+1​∣Ωt​)]), with the conditioning bar inside the argument of VVV; the form above follows the Bellman equation. At each parameter guess the value function is obtained in two steps: first the stationary fixed point of the Bellman equation with all current and future CSI subsidies at zero, which holds after the program ends, and then backward induction through the months of the program.

Several objects are fixed rather than estimated. The discount factor is not estimated (the paper cites Magnac and Thesmar 2002 on its weak identification): it is set to β=0.99\beta=0.99β=0.99 per month, an annual discount rate of about 12 percent. When a common consideration probability is estimated the point estimate is 0.0660 but imprecise, so it is imposed that 6.6 percent of households have ζi=1\zeta_i=1ζi​=1, independently of characteristics. The cost process is estimated separately from observed costs:

Ci,t+1=6.468×10−4+0.9925×Cit+ωit(25)C_{i,t+1}=6.468\times10^{-4}+0.9925\times C_{it}+\omega_{it} \tag{25}Ci,t+1​=6.468×10−4+0.9925×Cit​+ωit​(25)

with a standard deviation of ωit\omega_{it}ωit​ of 0.1611.

Because applications report zip codes but not demographics, adopters and non-adopters are counted by demographic bin (radiation quintiles, four home-value bins, three education bins) in each utility and month, assuming that adoptions within a zip code are spread randomly across the bins of each block group, in the spirit of Nevo (2001) and Berry et al. (2004). The cost coefficient is identified from utility-month variation in net cost, which comes from the subsidy steps (at different dates in each utility), technological progress, input costs and exchange rates; the identifying assumption is that shocks to local adoption are uncorrelated with utility-level average cost, and there are no instruments. The distribution of values is identified from cross-sectional variation across more than 2,500 zip codes in adoption rates given cost. The demographic coefficients are not causal; they serve only to trace out the density of private values, which is what the regulator's problem requires. Standard errors are the square root of the inverse of the outer product of the Jacobian.

Key Estimates

  • Value of solar: constant −10.6419-10.6419−10.6419; radiation 4.7961 (per 10 kWh per square meter per day); electricity price 4.0510 (per dollar per kWh); log home value in millions 0.7711; years of schooling 0.0986; SCE 0.2885 and SDG&E 1.2944 relative to PG&E; time trend 0.1247 and its square −0.0021-0.0021−0.0021. The average considering household has a negative value, which reflects large non-monetary costs of installing. Across the range of the data, radiation and electricity prices each shift the index by about 1.07 to 1.09, against 0.59 for education and a reported 0.54 for home value (a figure that requires base-10 logarithms; with the natural logarithms used in the adjacent footnote of the paper it would be 1.24), so the economics of offsetting expensive electricity dominate.

  • Cost sensitivity: with cost in units of 10,000 dollars, the coefficients are −0.5175-0.5175−0.5175 (cost), −0.1105-0.1105−0.1105 (cost times log home value) and −0.0300-0.0300−0.0300 (cost times years of schooling). Sensitivity rises with home value and schooling, probably because such households install larger systems and time their purchases better.

  • Elasticities: a 10 percent increase in the first period's subsidy raises total installations over the life of the program by 0.5 percent, and a 10 percent increase in every period raises them by 4.2 percent, in line with price elasticities of −0.42-0.42−0.42 to −0.85-0.85−0.85 in Pless and van Benthem (2019). Without any subsidy, installations would have been 60 percent lower (53 percent in Hughes and Podolefsky 2015).

  • Fit statistics: log-likelihood −268,399-268{,}399−268,399 over 41 months.

The cost coefficients imply the household-specific marginal utility of money:

αi=−0.5175−0.1105×log⁡(home valuei)−0.0300×schoolingi(26)\alpha_i=-0.5175-0.1105\times\log(\text{home value}_i)-0.0300\times\text{schooling}_i \tag{26}αi​=−0.5175−0.1105×log(home valuei​)−0.0300×schoolingi​(26)

with home value in millions of dollars and schooling in years.

Counterfactuals: The Efficient Subsidy

The regulator's benefit B(⋅)B(\cdot)B(⋅) is calibrated to the social value of solar electricity, including displaced emissions, from Baker et al. (2013), with concavity reflecting the falling marginal value of intermittent generation as in Gowrisankaran et al. (2016); a separate calculation based on a social cost of carbon is not reported. She must reach 0.68 percent adoption in 41 months, as the actual policy did. Four cases cross household foresight with technology improving as in the data or held at its initial level (which also removes the time trend). All spending and surplus figures are present values.

  • Spending: 495 million dollars (myopic, constant technology), 24 million (myopic, improving), 514 million (forward looking, constant) and 120 million (forward looking, improving), or 3.7, 0.2, 3.8 and 0.9 dollars per watt.

  • Subsidy path: the efficient subsidy rises in all four cases, from 3.6 to 5.6, 0.0 to 0.6, 3.8 to 5.7, and 0.6 to 1.5 dollars per watt respectively, against the CSI path that fell from 2.50 to zero.

  • Cost of foresight: foresight raises spending by 19 million dollars (4 percent) with constant technology and by 96 million dollars (397 percent) with improving technology, because the subsidy must compensate households for giving up an option to adopt later that is especially valuable when costs are falling.

  • Role of technical change: the regulator's spending falls by 95 percent with myopic households and by only 77 percent with forward-looking ones. With myopic households she delays the subsidy for several months (without any subsidy adoption would reach 0.62 percent, against 0.45 percent with forward-looking households) and substitutes technological progress for spending.

  • Consumer surplus: without a subsidy it is 26, 176, 84 and 918 million dollars in the four cases, and with the efficient subsidy 202, 194, 304 and 1,013 million. The program raises myopic surplus by 175 (18) million with constant (improving) technology and forward-looking surplus by 219 (95) million. Under the efficient subsidy, technical change lowers myopic surplus by nearly 8 million and raises forward-looking surplus by over 700 million: foresight forces the regulator to share the gains from cheaper technology.

  • Gains from optimal dynamics: relative to the unique constant subsidy that meets the target, the efficient schedule saves 3.4 percent (myopic) and 2.9 percent (forward looking) with constant technology, and 7.8 percent (myopic) and 1.9 percent (forward looking) with improving technology. Spending under the actual declining CSI schedule is not reported for comparison.

  • Decomposition: evaluated with fixed preferences, deterministic technology and fixed electricity prices, the price discrimination channel dominates for myopic households with constant technology; for forward-looking households the constrained channel starts at zero and grows slowly; technical change strengthens price discrimination but makes the smooth spending channel strongly negative, flattening the path; the adoption benefit channel is negligible.

Comparison with the Actual CSI Schedule

All cases here use forward-looking households and improving technology. If every observed cost decline is attributed to past adoption in California (extreme induced technical change), the efficient subsidy rises at first and is then roughly flat. Adding peer effects calibrated to Bollinger and Gillingham (2012) makes it eventually decline slightly. Attributing the whole estimated time trend to peer effects as well makes the subsidy decline, but far more slowly than the CSI did, and raises its initial level and total cost. Costs falling twice as fast leave the shape unchanged. Halving the regulator's discount rate still gives an increasing subsidy. A much more convex cost of funds (the spending level at which the cost of funds doubles reduced to 0.1 percent of its baseline value) or a tenfold marginal benefit of adoption yields a mildly declining subsidy, and cutting the discount rate by 90 percent acts like the tenfold benefit; a linear cost of funds changes little. Only a 50-fold marginal benefit of adoption generates a sharply declining path like the actual one, driven by the adoption benefit channel: the regulator then wants solar electricity early even at a high early subsidy. The cases with a higher marginal benefit are also the only ones in which the regulator's maximized value is positive, so under the baseline calibration a welfare-maximizing regulator would choose a much smaller target than the one California pursued.

This equation splits household iii's private value of owning the technology in period ttt into a systematic part and a shock. The term hith_{it}hit​ is the deterministic component: it collects household characteristics (demographics, location) and technology characteristics (quality) and may change over time. The term εi1t\varepsilon_{i1t}εi1t​ is an idiosyncratic preference shock attached to the alternative "adopt" (the subscript 1), drawn afresh every period. The value vitv_{it}vit​ is a stock, not a flow: it is the expected present value of everything the household gets from owning the technology from ttt onward, plus any one-time non-monetary benefit or cost of installing, so it is measured in the same units as the up-front cost C(t,Qt,ωt)C(t,Q_t,\omega_t)C(t,Qt​,ωt​) and the subsidy sts_tst​.

The additive form is what makes the stopping problem in equation (2) a standard binary choice between hit−C+st+εi1th_{it}-C+s_t+\varepsilon_{i1t}hit​−C+st​+εi1t​ and a continuation value plus εi0t\varepsilon_{i0t}εi0t​; with extreme-value shocks it delivers the logit probability in equation (23). It rules out shocks that scale with the value or that are correlated over time. In the theory section the shock is switched off and the value is a fixed number viv_ivi​ with distribution FFF, which is what lets the regulator rank households by a single type in equation (7). In the application hith_{it}hit​ is parameterized as Xit′γX_{it}'\gammaXit′​γ in equation (20).

This is the Bellman equation of a household that has not yet adopted. Adoption is an irreversible, once-only decision, so the problem is one of optimal stopping. The first argument of the maximum is the payoff from stopping now: systematic value hith_{it}hit​, minus the cost C(t,Qt,ωt)C(t,Q_t,\omega_t)C(t,Qt​,ωt​), plus the subsidy sts_tst​, plus the shock εi1t\varepsilon_{i1t}εi1t​; after adopting the household leaves the market, so nothing follows. The second argument is the payoff from waiting: the shock εi0t\varepsilon_{i0t}εi0t​ today plus the discounted expected value of facing the same choice tomorrow. The expectation is taken over next period's state Ωt+1\Omega_{t+1}Ωt+1​ (cost shock, subsidy, characteristics) and next period's shocks ε⃗i(t+1)\vec{\varepsilon}_{i(t+1)}εi(t+1)​, conditional on today's information Ωt\Omega_tΩt​; today's shocks do not help predict tomorrow's because they are independent over time.

The discount factor β∈[0,1)\beta\in[0,1)β∈[0,1) indexes foresight. With β=0\beta=0β=0 the continuation term vanishes and the household adopts as soon as hit−C+st+εi1t≥εi0th_{it}-C+s_t+\varepsilon_{i1t}\geq\varepsilon_{i0t}hit​−C+st​+εi1t​≥εi0t​ (myopia). With β>0\beta>0β>0 the household compares adopting now with the option value of adopting later at a lower cost or a higher subsidy, which is the source of the incentive constraint in equation (8). This is the regulator's date-0 objective in the general discrete-time setting. Two curvature assumptions drive the results. GGG is strictly increasing and strictly convex, so one dollar of spending costs more than one dollar in periods of high spending; this creates the smooth spending channel. BBB is weakly increasing and weakly concave, so adoption is worth more the earlier it occurs; this creates the adoption benefit channel. Household surplus is not in the objective, which is why the solution is called efficient and not optimal. With B′=0B'=0B′=0 and GGG linear the problem reduces to minimizing ∑t(1+r)−tst[Qt+1−Qt]\sum_t(1+r)^{-t}s_t[Q_{t+1}-Q_t]∑t​(1+r)−tst​[Qt+1​−Qt​], the mirror image of a durable-goods monopolist's profit maximization. The continuous-time counterpart of this objective is equation (10).

The marginal household at date ttt has value Y(t)Y(t)Y(t) and, by definition, finds ttt its optimal adoption date. Apply the first-order condition, equation (5), with vi=Y(t)v_i=Y(t)vi​=Y(t) and Ψi=t\Psi_i=tΨi​=t:

This equation is not printed in the paper; it is the δ→∞\delta\to\inftyδ→∞ limit of equation (8), and the paper states the result in words (perfectly impatient households adopt as soon as their net benefit is positive). Divide equation (8) by δ\deltaδ and rearrange:

The limit is consistent with the household problem. With δ=∞\delta=\inftyδ=∞ a household ignores the future, so it adopts at the first date at which vi−C(t,Q(t))+s(t)≥0v_i-C(t,Q(t))+s(t)\geq0vi​−C(t,Q(t))+s(t)≥0, and the type that becomes willing at ttt is Y(t)=C(t,Q(t))−s(t)Y(t)=C(t,Q(t))-s(t)Y(t)=C(t,Q(t))−s(t). This is the regulator's objective after the change of variables of equation (7), and it is the continuous-time version of equation (3). The discount factor (1+r)−t(1+r)^{-t}(1+r)−t becomes e−rte^{-rt}e−rt. The stock of adoption is Q(t)=1−F(Y(t))Q(t)=1-F(Y(t))Q(t)=1−F(Y(t)), so the flow benefit is B(1−F(Y(t)))B(1-F(Y(t)))B(1−F(Y(t))). The control is y(t)y(t)y(t), the speed at which the marginal type falls, and the single free parameter s0s_0s0​ is the initial subsidy. The subsidy path itself is not a control: given Y(⋅)Y(\cdot)Y(⋅) it is determined by the incentive constraint in equation (11) up to its initial value. This is the standard device of screening problems, in which the principal chooses the allocation and the transfers follow from incentive compatibility. Note how y(t)y(t)y(t) enters: linearly inside GGG, multiplied by s(t)f(Y(t))s(t)f(Y(t))s(t)f(Y(t)). If GGG were linear the integrand would be linear in the control and the solution could be bang-bang; strict convexity of GGG makes the Hamiltonian strictly concave in y(t)y(t)y(t) whenever s(t)>0s(t)>0s(t)>0. The necessary conditions of this problem are derived at equations (13) and (15).

These are the two laws of motion and the control constraint of the regulator's problem in equation (10). The first line defines the control: Y(t)Y(t)Y(t), the marginal type, is a state variable whose rate of change y(t)y(t)y(t) the regulator chooses. The restriction y(t)≤0y(t)\leq0y(t)≤0 is irreversibility: by equation (7), Q˙(t)=−f(Y(t))y(t)\dot{Q}(t)=-f(Y(t))y(t)Q˙​(t)=−f(Y(t))y(t), and adoption cannot be undone. The paper requires y(t)=0y(t)=0y(t)=0 at instants at which the regulator chooses to have no adoption.

The second line is the incentive constraint of equation (8) with Q(t)Q(t)Q(t) replaced by 1−F(Y(t))1-F(Y(t))1−F(Y(t)). It makes the subsidy s(t)s(t)s(t) a second state variable. Written out, the total derivative of cost is

The sign structure is informative. The coefficient δ\deltaδ on s(t)s(t)s(t) is positive, so the equation is unstable forward in time: it is naturally solved backward from the terminal condition in equation (12), which is how a promise about late subsidies feeds into all earlier subsidies. This backward dependence is the formal source of the time inconsistency of the plan and of the costate μ(t)\mu(t)μ(t) whose law of motion is equation (15).

The estimates illustrate the reading. This defines the money the household actually pays up front. CitC_{it}Cit​ is the pre-subsidy cost of a system of the median size (5.4 kilowatts) in household iii's utility in month ttt, in units of 10,000 dollars in the estimation. ϕ\phiϕ is the share of cost covered by the federal investment tax credit, 30 percent in this period, so (1−ϕ)Cit(1-\phi)C_{it}(1−ϕ)Cit​ is the cost after the federal credit. sits_{it}sit​ is the California Solar Initiative rebate for the same system in that utility and month. The index iii on cost and subsidy only records the household's utility.

The form encodes two assumptions. The federal credit is proportional to the gross cost, while the state rebate is a lump sum per watt, so the two enter differently: a one-dollar fall in CitC_{it}Cit​ lowers net cost by only 1−ϕ1-\phi1−ϕ dollars, while a one-dollar rise in sits_{it}sit​ lowers it by one dollar. The definition applies the federal share to the gross cost and not to cost net of the rebate. And the rebate is assumed to reach the household in full (complete pass-through), so the installer's price does not respond to it.

Net cost enters utility as αiC~it\alpha_i\tilde{C}_{it}αi​C~it​ with αi<0\alpha_i<0αi​<0 in equation (23), so the model restricts households to respond identically to a dollar of cost reduction after the federal credit and a dollar of subsidy. This restriction is what allows subsidy counterfactuals to be computed from a coefficient that is identified from all utility-by-month variation in net cost, including the stepwise declines of sits_{it}sit​ that occur at different dates in different utilities. In the theory the corresponding object is net cost z(t)=C(t,Q(t))−s(t)z(t)=C(t,Q(t))-s(t)z(t)=C(t,Q(t))−s(t).

This is the law of motion that households use to forecast system cost. It is a first-order autoregression: next month's cost equals an intercept κ0\kappa_0κ0​ plus κ1\kappa_1κ1​ times this month's cost plus a normally distributed shock ωit\omega_{it}ωit​ with mean zero. The index iii again only records the utility. Cost is the one stochastic state variable of the household's dynamic problem; the subsidy path, electricity prices and the time trend are deterministic functions of the month and are assumed known.

The specification makes two substantive assumptions. First, cost is exogenous: it does not depend on cumulative adoption QtQ_tQt​, so the estimated model sets C2=0C_2=0C2​=0 and shuts down the endogenous cost channel of equation (13); induced technical change and peer effects are brought back only in the counterfactuals. On notation: the note's continuation term E[V(Ωt+1,ε⃗i(t+1))∣Ωt]\mathbb{E}[V(\Omega_{t+1},\vec{\varepsilon}_{i(t+1)})\mid\Omega_t]E[V(Ωt+1​,εi(t+1)​)∣Ωt​] equals E[Vˉ(Ωt+1)∣Ωt]\mathbb{E}[\bar{V}(\Omega_{t+1})\mid\Omega_t]E[Vˉ(Ωt+1​)∣Ωt​] and is the correct object from the Bellman equation. The paper's likelihood prints the term with the conditioning bar inside the argument of VVV and without the shocks, which is a typographical slip. The symbol PitP_{it}Pit​ does not appear in the paper. In the logit the scale of utility is normalized by the shocks, and αi<0\alpha_i<0αi​<0 converts money into that scale.

Consider household iii among the NtN_tNt​ households that have not installed before month ttt. It is one of two permanent types: able to consider solar or not. Let ζi\zeta_iζi​ be the probability that it is able to consider solar. A household that cannot consider solar never adopts. A household that can consider solar adopts in ttt with probability PitP_{it}Pit​ from equation (23). By the law of total probability,

Pr⁡(i adopts in t)=ζiPit+(1−ζi)⋅0=ζiPit\Pr(i\text{ adopts in }t)=\zeta_iP_{it}+(1-\zeta_i)\cdot0=\zeta_iP_{it}Pr(i adopts in t)=ζi​Pit​+(1−ζi​)⋅0=ζi​Pit​
Pr⁡(i does not adopt in t)=(1−ζi)⋅1+ζi(1−Pit)\Pr(i\text{ does not adopt in }t)=(1-\zeta_i)\cdot1+\zeta_i(1-P_{it})Pr(i does not adopt in t)=(1−ζi​)⋅1+ζi​(1−Pit​)

The two probabilities sum to one. The shocks are independent across households, so the likelihood of the month is the product over households of the probability of what each one did, which can be written with indicator exponents:

Lt=∏i=1Nt{[ζiPit]1{i adopts in t}[(1−ζi)+ζi(1−Pit)]1{i does not adopt in t}}L_t=\prod_{i=1}^{N_t}\Big\{\left[\zeta_iP_{it}\right]^{1\{i\text{ adopts in }t\}}\left[(1-\zeta_i)+\zeta_i(1-P_{it})\right]^{1\{i\text{ does not adopt in }t\}}\Big\}Lt​=i=1∏Nt​​{[ζi​Pit​]1{i adopts in t}[(1−ζi​)+ζi​(1−Pit​)]1{i does not adopt in t}}

This matches the paper's likelihood once 1−Pit1-P_{it}1−Pit​ is recognized as the ratio with exp⁡(β E[V∣Ωt])\exp(\beta\,\mathbb{E}[V\mid\Omega_t])exp(βE[V∣Ωt​]) in the numerator. The full likelihood is the product of LtL_tLt​ over the months of the window.

How the 6.6 percent enters. When a common consideration probability is estimated freely the point estimate is 0.0660 but imprecise, so the paper fixes it: 6.6 percent of the households that have not installed at the start of the window have ζi=1\zeta_i=1ζi​=1, independently of characteristics. Since the econometrician does not observe who these households are, each household's contribution uses a consideration probability of 0.066 and not an indicator. The share acts as a ceiling on adoption: without it, the low observed adoption rate (0.68 percent over the window) would have to be explained by very low values alone.

One point is left implicit in both the paper and the note. Because the type is permanent, the product of the monthly terms is the exact likelihood of a household's history only if ζi\zeta_iζi​ in month ttt is read as the probability of being a considerer conditional on not having adopted before ttt. With initial share ζ\zetaζ this is

ζit=ζ∏τ<t(1−Piτ)(1−ζ)+ζ∏τ<t(1−Piτ)\zeta_{it}=\frac{\zeta\prod_{\tau<t}(1-P_{i\tau})}{(1-\zeta)+\zeta\prod_{\tau<t}(1-P_{i\tau})}ζit​=(1−ζ)+ζ∏τ<t​(1−Piτ​)ζ∏τ<t​(1−Piτ​)​

which declines over time as considerers adopt and leave. With this updating the monthly terms telescope to the mixture likelihood, ζ∏τ<t(1−Piτ)Pit\zeta\prod_{\tau<t}(1-P_{i\tau})P_{it}ζ∏τ<t​(1−Piτ​)Pit​ for a household adopting in ttt. Holding the share at 0.066 in every month is an approximation; it is mild here, because only about a tenth of considerers adopt within the window, so the share among remaining households falls from 6.6 to roughly 6 percent. The main text does not say which version is used; the paper refers to its Appendix B.3 for the serial correlation that ζi\zeta_iζi​ introduces.

These are the estimates of the cost process of equation (22), reported in the paper's footnote 35: κ0=6.468×10−4\kappa_0=6.468\times10^{-4}κ0​=6.468×10−4, κ1=0.9925\kappa_1=0.9925κ1​=0.9925, and a standard deviation of the shock ωit\omega_{it}ωit​ of 0.1611. They are obtained from the observed monthly utility-level cost series, outside the likelihood. The footnote does not state units; the natural reading is the unit used for cost elsewhere in the estimation, 10,000 dollars per system of 5.4 kilowatts.

The numbers imply a slow, noisy decline. The expected monthly change is

E[Ci,t+1−Cit∣Cit]=6.468×10−4−0.0075×Cit\mathbb{E}\left[C_{i,t+1}-C_{it}\mid C_{it}\right]=6.468\times10^{-4}-0.0075\times C_{it}E[Ci,t+1​−Cit​∣Cit​]=6.468×10−4−0.0075×Cit​

so with a negligible intercept cost is expected to fall by about 0.75 percent per month, or 1−0.992512≈8.61-0.9925^{12}\approx8.61−0.992512≈8.6 percent per year. The implied long-run level, κ0/(1−κ1)=6.468×10−4/0.0075≈0.086\kappa_0/(1-\kappa_1)=6.468\times10^{-4}/0.0075\approx0.086κ0​/(1−κ1​)=6.468×10−4/0.0075≈0.086, is close to zero relative to observed costs, so within the sample the process is essentially geometric decay. The half-life of a deviation is ln⁡0.5/ln⁡0.9925≈92\ln0.5/\ln0.9925\approx92ln0.5/ln0.9925≈92 months, longer than the estimation window. On the reading in units of 10,000 dollars, a system costing 4 units is expected to become about 300 dollars cheaper next month, while the shock has a standard deviation of about 1,600 dollars, so month-to-month forecasts are dominated by noise and the value of waiting comes from the cumulative drift.

These parameters matter for the results because they determine the option value of waiting in equation (23): the persistent expected decline is what makes forward-looking households costly to subsidize in the counterfactuals with improving technology.

This equation is not printed in the paper. It assembles the three coefficients in the lower panel of the paper's Table 2 (cost, cost times log home value, cost times years of schooling) into the household-specific coefficient that multiplies net cost C~it\tilde{C}_{it}C~it​ in equation (23). Because utility contains αiC~it\alpha_i\tilde{C}_{it}αi​C~it​ and the table interacts cost with the two demographics, collecting terms gives

αiC~it=[−0.5175−0.1105×log⁡(home valuei)−0.0300×schoolingi]C~it\alpha_i\tilde{C}_{it}=\left[-0.5175-0.1105\times\log(\text{home value}_i)-0.0300\times\text{schooling}_i\right]\tilde{C}_{it}αi​C~it​=[−0.5175−0.1105×log(home valuei​)−0.0300×schoolingi​]C~it​

with cost in units of 10,000 dollars, home value in millions of dollars and schooling in years. The assembly is correct. Table 2 marks the three coefficients with three, two and one stars, although the reported standard errors (0.2416, 0.0732, 0.0154) give t-ratios of only about 2.1, 1.5 and 1.9.

Which logarithm is meant is not settled by the paper, because two footnotes contradict each other. Footnote 42 computes the effect of home value on the value of solar as 0.7711×(log⁡1−log⁡0.2)=0.53900.7711\times(\log1-\log0.2)=0.53900.7711×(log1−log0.2)=0.5390, which is true only in base 10 (0.7711×0.6990=0.53900.7711\times0.6990=0.53900.7711×0.6990=0.5390; with natural logs the product is 0.7711×1.6094=1.24100.7711\times1.6094=1.24100.7711×1.6094=1.2410). For the average household in the paper's Table 1 (home value 0.4765 million dollars, 13.6 years of schooling) the two readings give

αi=−0.5175−0.1105×ln⁡(0.4765)−0.0300×13.6=−0.5175+0.0819−0.4080=−0.8436\alpha_i=-0.5175-0.1105\times\ln(0.4765)-0.0300\times13.6=-0.5175+0.0819-0.4080=-0.8436αi​=−0.5175−0.1105×ln(0.4765)−0.0300×13.6=−0.5175+0.0819−0.4080=−0.8436

Either way roughly half of the cost sensitivity of a typical household comes from the schooling interaction. If natural logs are the ones used in estimation, the statement that home value shifts the value of solar by about half as much as radiation or electricity prices does not hold: its range effect, 1.2410, exceeds theirs.
